extracted.intended_audience: attorneys who practice before the USPTO, OED practitioners, and adjudicators in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for proving misconduct and imposing sanctions in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) proceedings, including applicable statutes, PTO Rules of Professional Conduct, summary judgment standards, burden of proof, and sanctioning guidance. Useful for evaluating alleged violations (e.g., failure to pay court-ordered sanction, failure to cooperate with OED) and determining appropriate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority for discipline (35 U.S.C. § 32 and § 2(b)(2)(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO may suspend or exclude from practice any attorney shown to be incompetent or disreputable, guilty of gross misconduct, or who does not comply with regulations established under 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D). The PTO has plenary authority to govern conduct of attorneys who practice before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites Kroll v. Finnerty to underscore broad authority. The statutory language is construed broadly to permit regulation of recognition and conduct of those representing applicants before the Office; this may reach conduct occurring outside the PTO where relevant to fitness to practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101–11.901)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO codified Rules of Professional Conduct, effective May 3, 2013, based on the ABA Model Rules, intended to align with state professional responsibility rules while addressing practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO Rules may be interpreted with reference to ABA Model Rules and state opinions; specific provisions referenced in the decision include §§ 11.1 (scope/definitions), 11.22 (RFI), 11.304, 11.49 (burden), 11.54 (sanction factors), 11.801(b), and 11.804.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard (FRCP 56(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A court shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FRCP 56(c)(1) requires supporting assertions with particular materials (depositions, documents, ESI, affidavits, stipulations, admissions, interrogatory answers, etc.). FRCP 56(e) authorizes remedies (opportunity to support facts, deem facts undisputed, grant summary judgment, or other appropriate orders) where a party fails to properly support or address facts. Apply Anderson v. Liberty Lobby: 'material' = affects outcome under governing law; 'genuine' = reasonable jury could return verdict for nonmoving party. In OED proceedings, summary judgment inquiry accounts for any applicable evidentiary burdens (e.g., clear and convincing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in OED proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the violation by clear and convincing evidence; a respondent bears the burden of proving any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the 'clear and convincing' standard applies, the summary judgment question is whether the evidence is such that a jury applying that standard could reasonably find for either party (Liberty Lobby cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to establish violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a violation of § 11.304(c) (fairness to opposing party and counsel — 'Knowingly disobey an obligation under the rules of a tribunal'), the OED Director must show: (1) the person is a practitioner; (2) there was an obligation under the rules of a tribunal; (3) the practitioner disobeyed that obligation; (4) the disobedience was knowing; and (5) there was no open refusal based on an assertion that no valid obligation existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule's heading and preamble suggest a focus on marshaling evidence fairly (analogous to ABA Model Rule 3.4). 'Tribunal' includes courts (37 C.F.R. § 11.1). 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge and may be inferred from circumstances. Case law applying Model Rule counterparts supports applying the rule to failure to comply with court orders (e.g., child support, court-ordered costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'tribunal' and 'knowingly' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tribunal' is defined to include a court. 'Knowingly' is defined as actual knowledge of the fact in question, and knowledge may be inferred from circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitional rules when assessing whether an element of a PTO Rule is met (e.g., whether failure to follow a court order was 'knowing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct for failing to cooperate with disciplinary authority (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who knowingly fails to cooperate with OED in an investigation or to respond to lawful demands for information from a disciplinary authority engages in professional misconduct under § 11.801(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to an RFI and subsequent Lack of Response letters, despite receipt, supports this charge. State and federal decisions treat noncooperation as serious misconduct and often intentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct definitions in § 11.804 (prejudicial conduct and fitness to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: § 11.804(d) makes it professional misconduct to 'engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.' § 11.804(i) covers 'other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner’s fitness to practice before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions are aggregate misbehavior catch-alls; failure to obey a court order or to cooperate with disciplinary investigations can fall within these subsections when they reflect adversely on integrity or fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of PTO disciplinary authority (interpretive standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO disciplinary authority can reach practitioner conduct related to representation before the Office even if the conduct occurs outside of a PTO proceeding (e.g., in a state court action arising from PTO-related representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (Kroll, Bender) and regulatory language (37 C.F.R. § 11.1) support a broad reach; PTO may discipline for conduct reflecting potential to repeat with future clients. The authority does not require prior state discipline or a state court sanction for PTO to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Model Rule 3.4 and its comments as interpretive aid
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO Rules were based on ABA Model Rules; comments to Model Rule 3.4 and state interpretations provide guidance for interpreting 37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model Rule 3.4 comments discuss marshaling evidence fairly, prohibitions on destruction/ concealment of evidence, improper influence of witnesses, obstructive tactics in discovery, falsifying evidence, and the like — analogous conduct can violate PTO Rule 11.304.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) sets factors to consider in imposing discipline: whether misconduct violated duties owed to client/public/legal system/profession; the practitioner's mental state (intentional/knowing/negligent); amount of actual or potential injury; and other factors including aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators should evaluate culpability, injury, prior discipline, obstruction of disciplinary proceedings, remorse/recognition, length of practice, and restitution/indifference. These factors are applied in light of ABA Standards guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards for Imposition of Lawyer Sanctions (disbarment vs suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards provide benchmarks: disbarment is generally appropriate when a lawyer knowingly violates a court order or rule with intent to obtain a benefit for the lawyer and causes serious or potentially serious injury; suspension is generally appropriate when knowledge of violation causes injury or potential injury but not rise to disbarment-level harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific citations used: §§ 6.21, 6.22 (violation of court order), §§ 7.1, 7.2 (violation of duty owed as professional), § 8.1(b) (repeat misconduct after suspension) — use these to calibrate sanctions in conjunction with § 11.54(b) factors and aggravators/mitigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (examples used by adjudicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include prior disciplinary offenses, dishonest or selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, bad faith obstruction of proceedings (failure to cooperate), lack of remorse, experience in practice, and indifference to restitution. Mitigating factors include personal/emotional problems, mental illness, chemical dependency, or other evidence of rehabilitation (none present here).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating circumstances can raise sanction severity (toward exclusion/disbarment), especially where respondent has prior similar suspension; absence of mitigating evidence supports harsher sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rules on motions and responses (37 C.F.R. § 11.43 and prehearing order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions, including summary judgment motions, are governed by 37 C.F.R. § 11.43; the hearing officer sets time periods for filing responses. The prehearing order here required responses within 15 calendar days; late responses require a motion for leave and showing of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicator may accept late filings in the interest of justice where no prejudice to the movant results; but failure to file timely without good cause can be sanctionable and factual assertions in late oppositions may be disregarded if unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRCP 56(c)(1) acceptable supporting materials
rubrics_metrics.description: A party asserting that a fact cannot be or is genuinely disputed must support the assertion by citing particular materials in the record, including depositions, documents, electronically stored information, affidavits or declarations, stipulations, admissions, interrogatory answers, or other materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding summary judgment motions in OED proceedings, the adjudicator may rely on analogous FRCP guidance to evaluate whether assertions are properly supported. Unsupported assertions or mere denials are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing 'material' and 'genuine' disputes (Anderson v. Liberty Lobby)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Material' facts are those that might affect the outcome under governing law. A dispute is 'genuine' when the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing summary judgment, evidence of the nonmovant is to be believed and all justifiable inferences drawn in favor of the nonmovant; nonetheless, merely colorable or not sufficiently probative evidence does not preclude summary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failing to support or address facts on summary judgment (FRCP 56(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to properly support an assertion of fact or to properly address another party’s assertion as required by Rule 56(c), the court may: give an opportunity to properly support or address the fact; consider the fact undisputed for purposes of the motion; grant summary judgment if the motion and supporting materials (including undisputed facts) show entitlement; or issue any other appropriate order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In OED proceedings, failure to properly address factual assertions can lead to granting summary judgment; this is particularly significant where the movant bears the burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence and the nonmovant fails to raise material disputes.
